clinicalPearls: A stretch-induced disorder of the spinal cord, typically from a low-lying conus medullaris and/or a thickened, fatty, or tight filum terminale
Often associated with spinal dysraphism such as lipomyelomeningocele, dermal sinus, split-cord malformation, or a fatty filum
Cutaneous stigmata over the lower back (a hairy patch or hypertrichosis, a dimple or sinus, a lipoma, a haemangioma, or a skin tag) are important clues, especially in children
Children may present with delayed milestones, gait abnormality, foot deformity, scoliosis, limb or muscle asymmetry, and bladder dysfunction
Adults may present later with progressive back and leg pain, sensory and motor changes, and bladder, bowel, or sexual dysfunction, sometimes provoked by growth or activity
MRI typically shows the conus below the L1/2 level and/or a filum thicker than about 2 mm, often with a fatty filum
Urodynamic studies are valuable for detecting and monitoring neurogenic bladder involvement
Surgical detethering (release of the filum or untethering of the cord) aims to halt progression, and because established deficits may not fully reverse the timing of surgery is important
reference.pathophysiology: Tethered cord syndrome results from abnormal caudal fixation of the spinal cord so that it is placed under longitudinal traction. Normally the conus ascends to around the L1/2 level; when it is anchored, whether by a short, thick, or fatty filum terminale, a dysraphic lesion such as a lipoma, a dermal sinus tract, or a split-cord malformation, normal movement is restricted and the cord is stretched, particularly with growth and flexion. The resulting mechanical strain impairs neuronal metabolism and blood flow in the conus, producing progressive neurological, urological, and orthopaedic dysfunction, and overlying cutaneous stigmata reflect the associated dysraphism.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of neurogenic bladder in childhood
Cerebral palsy or another central cause of gait and limb abnormality
Lumbosacral disc or stenotic pathology in adults
Hereditary spastic paraplegia for progressive lower-limb signs
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the whole spine to show the conus level, filum thickness or fat, and any associated dysraphism
Urodynamic studies to assess and monitor bladder function
Examination and documentation of cutaneous stigmata over the spine
Neurophysiology such as lower-limb studies where indicated to characterise deficits
Plain radiographs or scoliosis imaging to assess associated bony deformity
redFlags: Progressive neurological deterioration such as weakness, sensory loss, or worsening gait
New or worsening bladder or bowel dysfunction
Rapidly progressive scoliosis or foot deformity in a child with cutaneous stigmata
reference.prognosis: Detethering usually arrests progression and often relieves pain; motor and sensory recovery is variable and bladder dysfunction may only stabilise rather than reverse, so outcomes are best when surgery is performed before significant fixed deficits develop. Re-tethering can occur and require further surgery.
pitfalls: Dismissing lumbosacral cutaneous stigmata that signal occult dysraphism
Delaying imaging in a child with unexplained gait, foot, or bladder problems
Expecting full reversal of long-standing deficits after detethering
references: Winn: Youmans and Winn Neurological Surgery
management: Microsurgical detethering — division of a tight or fatty filum terminale and untethering of the cord from any associated lipoma, dermal sinus or split-cord malformation — is the definitive treatment to relieve longitudinal traction
Operate before fixed neurological, urological or orthopaedic deficits develop, as this offers the best chance of arresting progression
Manage the neurogenic bladder with intermittent catheterisation and antimuscarinic therapy, guided by serial urodynamics
Symptomatic care with analgesia for back and leg pain, physiotherapy, and orthotic or surgical correction of foot deformity and scoliosis
Lifelong surveillance with periodic neurological examination, urodynamic studies and MRI to detect re-tethering
Multidisciplinary care coordinating neurosurgery, urology, orthopaedics and physiotherapy
Escalate promptly for repeat detethering if progressive motor, sensory or sphincter deterioration occurs
